question.text: The risk-free rate used in CAPM and DCF models in India is typically represented by:

answer.text: The repo rate set by RBI
The yield on 10-year Government of India securities (G-Sec)

explanation.text: The Logic: CAPM and DCF models both need a risk-free rate as their base. In Indian valuation practice, the yield on 10-year Government of India securities is the standard proxy: sovereign local-currency borrowing has no default risk, the 10-year tenor matches the typical equity valuation horizon, and the G-Sec yield is observable in liquid secondary markets. Hence the equity cost-of-capital "Rf" plug in Indian models is conventionally the 10-year G-Sec yield. The Trap: The repo rate is a short-term overnight policy rate set by RBI, not a long-horizon risk-free rate. SBI fixed-deposit rates are corporate-bank credit instruments and carry bank credit risk. The Nifty 50 dividend yield is an equity-market metric, not a risk-free benchmark. Note: The cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook pages reviewed in the audit support the general CAPM/DCF concept that a risk-free rate is required and that sovereign government borrowing has no default risk, but the specific "10-year G-Sec" proxy claim is not on the pages checked. The framing above reflects general Indian industry valuation practice.
